strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and timely problem: existing fidelity/coverage metrics (Density, Coverage, and many recent variants) lack robustness to outliers and interpretable absolute scores, an issue explicitly highlighted by a recent position paper (Räisä et al., 2025). The paper directly tackles this open challenge.

The proposed fixes are simple, principled, and well-motivated: capping individual sample contributions to 1 and clipping ball radii to the median NND for Clipped Density; using constant-mass balls with capped per-sample contribution for Clipped Coverage. The intuition is clearly illustrated with a toy example (Figure 2).

Rigorous theoretical treatment: Lemma 1 derives a closed-form expected value of ClippedCoverage_unnorm under the null (identical distributions) using a Beta-Binomial argument, which is then used to calibrate the metric for linear degradation. The proof is detailed and appears correct.

Extensive empirical validation across many controlled scenarios (mode dropping, OOD sample injection, distribution translation, mixture tests) on both synthetic and real (CIFAR-10) data, with comparisons against a large number of baselines (Precision/Recall, Density/Coverage, symPrecision/symRecall, α-Precision/β-Recall, TopP&R, P-precision/P-recall, Precision/Recall Cover). Clipped Density/Coverage are the only metrics passing all tests.

Strong reproducibility efforts: reimplementation details, complexity analysis showing improved memory scaling (O(Nd) vs O(N^2)), verification that reimplementations match original code outputs exactly, and detailed compute/resource reporting.

Thorough appendix material: real-world case studies (e.g., RESFLOW CIFAR-10 outliers inflating Density, chest X-ray GAN evaluation demonstrating absolute interpretability), a component-wise ablation (Table 3–6) isolating the effect of each modification, sensitivity analysis to hyperparameter k, and an honest, detailed comparison against the Räisä et al. sanity-check benchmark, including candid discussion of cases where the paper's own metrics fail or where they contest the benchmark's criteria.

Practical significance demonstrated via evaluation of many real generative models (CIFAR-10, ImageNet, LSUN, FFHQ) showing consistent, interpretable trends (diffusion > GAN, dataset-size correlation with achievable scores), illustrating real utility for practitioners assessing absolute model quality.
weaknesses: The interpretability claim ("score x means equivalent to x proportion of good samples") is calibrated specifically against a scenario of purely random/OOD 'bad' samples; it's unclear how this interpretation generalizes to more realistic failure modes (e.g., subtle mode collapse, minor distributional shift, blurry-but-plausible samples) rather than obviously out-of-distribution noise.

Clipped Coverage's calibration procedure (numerical inversion of fexpected via sorting, Section 4.2.2) is somewhat ad hoc/non-closed-form compared to Clipped Density's simpler real-data normalization; the general applicability and stability of this calibration across very different dataset sizes/dimensionalities is not deeply analyzed.

The paper's own benchmark comparison against Räisä et al. (2025) in Appendix H reveals a non-trivial number of failures for Clipped Density/Coverage (e.g., 'Discrete Num. vs Continuous Num.', 'Hypercube Varying Sample/Syn Size', several Bounds tests), and the paper argues some of the benchmark's failure criteria are 'too harsh' or 'incorrect' — this self-serving reinterpretation of failing cases could be seen as weakening the objectivity of the evaluation.

The choice of k (number of nearest neighbors) remains a manual hyperparameter; although Appendix K shows relative stability, no principled method for selecting k is proposed, and all main experiments use a single fixed k=5.

Reliance on a single embedding space (DINOv2-L) for all real-image experiments; the paper acknowledges but does not empirically explore sensitivity of Clipped Density/Coverage to the choice of embedding model, which is known to meaningfully affect metric rankings (per Stein et al. 2023).

No user study or downstream task validation connecting the proposed 'interpretable' scores to actual perceptual quality or practical utility judgments — the interpretability claim rests on synthetic calibration/definition rather than external validation.

Some presentation clutter: heavy reliance on an extensive appendix (37 pages) for core supporting evidence (e.g., proofs, ablations, benchmark comparisons) makes the main text feel like a summary of a much larger body of work, and readers must consult appendices extensively to fully evaluate claims.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated problem: the lack of robustness to outliers and lack of absolute interpretability in existing fidelity/coverage metrics for generative models.

Technically careful treatment: a rigorous derivation (Lemma 1, Appendix A) of the expected behavior of unnormalized Clipped Coverage under the null hypothesis, used to construct a calibration function.

Very thorough experimental section and appendix: many ablations (sensitivity to k, unnormalized plots, toy-dataset reproductions, chest X-ray case study, comparison to the Räisä et al. benchmark, implementation/runtime comparisons against original baseline code).
Clear illustrative failure-case analysis (Figure 2, Figure 7, RESFLOW case study) that concretely shows how existing Density/Coverage metrics can be fooled by over-occurring or outlier samples.
Reasonable efficiency/implementation contribution: reimplementation of several baselines with lower memory footprint and faster runtime, verified to match original outputs.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core idea (clipping individual sample contributions to at most 1, and clipping/fixing ball radii or mass) is an incremental extension of Density/Coverage (Naeem et al. 2020) and conceptually overlaps with existing fixes such as Precision/Recall Cover and symPrecision/symRecall; the main technical novelty is largely confined to the calibration procedure for Clipped Coverage.

The sanity-check tests used to argue superiority (Figures 1, 4, 5, and their toy-data analogues) are designed by the authors themselves and closely mirror the desiderata used to construct the metrics, raising concerns of circularity: the proposed metrics are almost guaranteed to pass tests that were built to match their own design principles, while competing metrics were not designed with these same criteria in mind.

When evaluated on an independent, pre-existing benchmark (Räisä et al. 2025, Appendix H), Clipped Density and Clipped Coverage still fail a substantial number of sanity checks, comparable to other metrics; the paper's response is to reclassify several of the benchmark's declared failures as 'harsh' or 'incorrect' criteria, which is a somewhat self-serving way to explain away unfavorable results rather than a neutral assessment.

The interpretability claim (score x = equivalent to x proportion of good samples) is in tension with the paper's own finding that the range of scores (and thus what counts as a 'good' absolute value) depends heavily on dataset size (e.g., CIFAR-10/FFHQ max ≈0.4 vs ImageNet max ≈1.0); this undermines the central selling point that absolute scores are universally interpretable across datasets.

Normalization of Clipped Density relies on an empirically computed real-data reference score (leave-one-out), making the metric's absolute scale implicitly dependent on dataset sample size, embedding space, and k, which is not rigorously analyzed or theoretically justified (unlike the coverage calibration, which at least has a derivation under an idealized i.i.d. assumption that may not hold for real, non-identically distributed data).

No human-centered or downstream-task validation is provided to substantiate that the proposed 'interpretable' scores actually correspond to meaningful practical judgments of model quality (e.g., in the chest X-ray case study, only a single model is evaluated with no comparison point, limiting the demonstrated practical utility).

The reliance on DINOv2 embeddings and k-NN ball constructions means the method inherits known high-dimensional nearest-neighbor pathologies (hubness), and while the paper cites this as motivation, it does not deeply analyze how embedding choice interacts with the proposed clipping scheme beyond using the recommended embedding model.

Computational and implementation complexity (in particular the numerical calibration procedure for Clipped Coverage, which requires precomputing a sorted table over M and is somewhat ad hoc/non-closed-form) somewhat reduces simplicity and reproducibility relative to the simplicity of the original Density/Coverage metrics.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and timely problem (robust, interpretable generative model evaluation), directly responding to the critique in the recent position paper (Räisä et al., 2025) that all current fidelity/diversity metrics are flawed.
Clean, principled method design: clipping individual sample contributions and ball radii/masses is intuitively motivated and clearly illustrated with toy examples (Fig. 2, 3).

Strong theoretical contribution: Lemma 1 derives a closed-form expected value for the uncalibrated Clipped Coverage metric under matched distributions (Beta-Binomial derivation), enabling principled calibration for linear interpretability rather than purely heuristic normalization.

Extensive and carefully designed empirical validation: multiple distinct stress tests (mode dropping, matched OOD injection, distribution translation, progressive bad-sample injection) on both synthetic Gaussian data and real CIFAR-10/DINOv2 embeddings, compared against a large set of 8+ baseline fidelity and coverage metrics.

High reproducibility effort: detailed implementation comparisons showing numerical equivalence with original baseline implementations, computational complexity analysis, runtime/memory benchmarking, and hyperparameter (k) sensitivity analysis.

Thorough appendix work, including direct evaluation on the recent Räisä et al. benchmark with transparent discussion of discrepancies and disagreements with that benchmark's criteria, and a practical real-world case study (chest X-ray GAN evaluation) demonstrating the value of absolute interpretability.

Broad real-dataset evaluation (CIFAR-10, ImageNet, LSUN Bedroom, FFHQ) across many generative model families (GANs, diffusion, consistency, transformer, VAE, normalizing flow), showing consistent and sensible relative ordering (diffusion > GAN) plus novel interpretable absolute-score insights.
weaknesses: The interpretability claim ('score x = proportion x of good/bad samples') is calibrated and validated specifically against a particular notion of 'bad' sample (i.i.d. OOD/noise injected uniformly); it is unclear how well this equivalence generalizes to more realistic, structured quality degradations (e.g., partial mode collapse, systematic texture artifacts, blur) rather than pure outlier injection.

The calibration procedure for Clipped Coverage (Section 4.2.2) relies on a somewhat ad hoc numerical inversion/lookup (sorting fexpected values to build g) rather than a closed-form correction, which is less elegant and whose behavior in edge cases (e.g., very small M, extreme k) is not deeply analyzed.

Nearly all validation scenarios are designed by the authors themselves (or adapted from Naeem et al.) specifically to probe the known weaknesses of baseline metrics; there is limited evidence that the proposed metrics better track actual perceptual/downstream quality differences between real generative models beyond self-consistency checks.

No human evaluation, downstream task performance, or correlation analysis with perceptual quality judgments is provided to validate that the 'interpretable' absolute scores (e.g., 0.4 on CIFAR-10) actually align with human-perceived notions of '40% good samples'.

Dependence on the embedding space (DINOv2) and the nearest-neighbor hyperparameter k remains a residual limitation; while sensitivity to k is shown to be comparatively mild, no principled way to select k is proposed.

The appendix (Section H) shows the metrics only pass roughly half of the sanity checks in the Räisä et al. benchmark, with the authors contesting some failing cases as being due to overly strict thresholds or 'incorrect' benchmark criteria — this self-adjudication slightly weakens the claim of comprehensively solving the problem identified by that benchmark.

strengths: Addresses a well-recognized and important problem: the lack of robust, interpretable fidelity/coverage metrics for generative models, directly responding to the recent position paper (Räisä et al., 2025) that argues all current metrics are flawed.

Clean, well-motivated methodological contribution: clipping individual sample contributions to bound outlier influence, plus clipping nearest-neighbor ball radii (for fidelity) to avoid large-volume outlier balls dominating the score.

Rigorous theoretical support: Lemma 1 derives the exact expected value of unnormalized Clipped Coverage under the i.i.d. null via a Beta-Binomial argument, enabling a principled empirical calibration that yields the desired linear degradation property, which is proven and clearly presented (Appendix A/B).

Extensive and carefully designed empirical validation: dozens of controlled synthetic/toy tests (mode dropping, mode collapse, outlier injection, distribution translation, rare modes, incorrect correlations), evaluation on four real image datasets with ~46 generative models, a medical imaging (chest X-ray) case study demonstrating absolute (reference-free) interpretability, human-judgment correlation analysis, sensitivity to hyperparameter k, sample-size stability analysis, and even non-image modalities (music, time series).

Strong reproducibility and transparency: detailed implementation/complexity comparisons against prior metric implementations (with exact score reproduction and efficiency gains), computational cost reporting, and code release.

Honest engagement with limitations and counter-evidence, including candidly reporting a non-significant correlation with human judgment on FFHQ and providing a detailed, self-critical comparison against the Räisä et al. benchmark rather than only favorable cherry-picked results.
The interpretability framing (score = proportion of good vs. bad samples) is intuitive and operationalized in a testable, quantitative way rather than left as a vague claim.
weaknesses: The core technical idea (clipping per-sample contributions to at most 1, and clipping ball radii to a median value) is an incremental, relatively simple modification of the existing Density/Coverage (PRDC) framework rather than a fundamentally new evaluation paradigm.

The central interpretability claim (linear score degradation with proportion of "bad" samples) is one particular, somewhat idiosyncratic notion of interpretability; the paper does not deeply justify why this specific desideratum should be the gold standard versus alternative interpretable calibrations.

The human-correlation validation, a key piece of evidence for real-world validity, fails to show significance on FFHQ for both metrics, weakening the empirical case for correlation with human perceptual judgment on one of the four benchmark datasets.

In the comparison to the Räisä et al. (2025) benchmark, several failures of Clipped Coverage are explained away by the authors' own reinterpretation of what should count as a "pass" (Sections H.1/H.2), which, while reasonably argued, is somewhat self-serving and could be viewed skeptically by readers who trust the original benchmark's criteria.

Calibration for Clipped Coverage assumes the i.i.d. real=synthetic setting to derive the reference curve; robustness of this calibration when N and M differ substantially, or under more complex non-outlier distributional mismatches, is not deeply analyzed theoretically (only empirically for a few settings).

The paper explicitly acknowledges the lack of an infinite-sample theoretical analysis and does not exhaustively characterize all failure cases, relying on an evolving/incomplete battery of sanity checks.

The manuscript is extremely long (57 pages) with the vast majority of substantive evidence relegated to appendices; the main body alone (10 pages) provides comparatively limited direct empirical evidence, which could hinder standalone readability, though the appendix content is strong when read in full.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and timely problem: existing fidelity/coverage metrics (Density, Coverage, Precision/Recall variants) are known to be biased by outliers and lack absolute interpretability, as highlighted by a recent position paper (Räisä et al., 2025). The paper proposes a concrete technical fix (clipping individual sample contributions and, for density, clipping ball radii) that is simple, well-motivated, and clearly explained with illustrative toy examples (Figure 2).

Provides a theoretical derivation (Lemma 1, Beta-Binomial expectation) for the calibration of Clipped Coverage, and an empirical leave-one-out calibration for Clipped Density, giving a principled basis for the claimed linear, interpretable degradation property.

Extremely thorough empirical validation: synthetic stress tests (mode dropping, OOD injection, translation, bad-sample mixtures) on both CIFAR-10 and toy Gaussian data; real-dataset evaluation across CIFAR-10, ImageNet, LSUN Bedroom, FFHQ, and even a medical (Chest X-ray) and music (FMA) dataset; sensitivity analyses for hyperparameter k, sample size N, and calibration stability; and comparison against ~10 baseline metrics with reproduced/reimplemented code.
Reasonable correlation with human judgment (Pearson r>0.8) on 3 of 4 real datasets, and honest reporting of the failure case on FFHQ rather than suppressing it.

Good engineering/reproducibility effort: implementation comparison table showing exact numerical agreement with original metric implementations, discussion of computational complexity (O(Nd) vs O(N^2)), and extensive appendix detailing compute budgets.

Directly engages with a recent, more rigorous external benchmark (Räisä et al.) rather than only self-designed tests, improving the credibility of the robustness claims, and candidly discusses discrepancies and disagreements with that benchmark's criteria.
weaknesses: The central interpretability claim ('a score of x indicates equivalent quality to a dataset with x proportion good and (1-x) bad samples') is only validated in a narrow, artificial setting where 'bad' samples are literally noise or clearly OOD points mixed in at known proportions. It is unclear this interpretation transfers to realistic generative model failure modes (e.g., subtle blur, mode under-representation, texture artifacts), where samples are not cleanly separable into 'good' and 'bad'. The claims of 'absolute interpretability' in the main text (e.g., Section 5.3, chest X-ray case study) may therefore be overstated relative to what was actually demonstrated.

On the authors' own reported results against the Räisä et al. (2025) benchmark (Tables 7-8, Appendix H), Clipped Density and Clipped Coverage still fail a substantial fraction of sanity checks, especially in the 'Bounds' category testing the [0,1] normalization property that is central to the paper's interpretability claims. The paper's post-hoc reclassification of some failures as 'harsh' or 'incorrect' criteria is only partly convincing and reduces confidence that the proposed metrics robustly satisfy their own stated desiderata.

The human-agreement validation (Appendix G), a key piece of evidence for practical validity, shows no significant correlation on the FFHQ dataset, one of only four datasets tested, which weakens the generality of the claim that the metrics track perceptual quality.

Clipped Density still depends on a hyperparameter k and on computing a reference 'ClippedDensity_real' via a leave-one-out procedure on the real set for normalization; this adds complexity and a potential source of variance/bias (dataset-size dependence) that is only partially explored (Appendix L/M) and could hinder straightforward comparability of absolute scores across papers using different real-data splits.

The core technical contribution (clipping contributions to at most 1, and clipping the ball radius to a median-based cap) is a relatively incremental modification of existing Density/Coverage metrics rather than a fundamentally new evaluation paradigm; novelty is moderate.

Some reported behaviors (e.g., Clipped Density exceeding 1 under guidance/truncation, Appendix K) require additional post-hoc explanation and further clipping decisions, suggesting the metric's behavior is not as cleanly bounded or intuitive in practice as the main paper's framing implies.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and timely problem: current fidelity/coverage metrics for generative models are known to be fragile to outliers and lack absolute interpretability (as highlighted by the cited position paper of Räisä et al. 2025). The paper proposes a principled fix via sample-contribution clipping and ball-radius clipping.

The two proposed metrics (Clipped Density, Clipped Coverage) are well motivated with clear intuitive failure-case illustrations (Figure 2) and are backed by both empirical calibration and a theoretical result (Lemma 1, with full proof in Appendix A) establishing the expected behavior of Clipped Coverage under matching distributions.

Extensive and carefully designed experimental validation: synthetic stress tests (mode dropping, mode collapse, outlier injection, distribution translation), real-dataset evaluations across CIFAR-10, ImageNet, LSUN-Bedroom and FFHQ with numerous generative model families, and toy-dataset replications that mirror the main experiments—providing convincing evidence the metrics behave as intended across varied settings.

Strong, largely self-critical and transparent appendix: comparisons against existing metric implementations for correctness and efficiency (Table 1), computational complexity analysis, sensitivity analysis to the hyperparameter k, calibration stability vs. sample size, trade-off/truncation experiments, and honest engagement with a recent adversarial benchmark (Räisä et al.) including disclosed discrepancies and justification for disagreements.

Demonstrates applied value beyond toy validation: correlation with human perceptual judgments (Figure 8), a no-reference-model medical imaging use case (Chest X-ray evaluation), and tests on additional modalities (music, time series), showing good generality.
Clear writing, well-organized structure, and apparent reproducibility (code availability, detailed implementation and dataset descriptions).
weaknesses: The central interpretability claim ("score x means equivalent to a dataset with proportion x good and (1-x) bad samples") is calibrated/validated mainly using synthetic noise/out-of-distribution samples as "bad" examples; it remains unclear how well this absolute interpretation generalizes to more realistic, structured forms of generative model imperfection rather than injected noise.

Clipped Coverage's calibration function g is derived under an i.i.d./matching-distribution assumption and computed numerically per (N, M, k); its behavior when the real and synthetic distributions genuinely differ (the practical use case) is justified mostly empirically rather than theoretically, leaving a gap between the theoretical guarantee and real-world applicability.

In the comparison against the Räisä et al. (2025) benchmark (Appendix H), several of the proposed metrics' failures are reinterpreted by the authors as artifacts of overly "harsh" or "incorrect" criteria; while plausible, this self-adjudicated reconciliation introduces a degree of subjectivity that a neutral referee might contest.

The method still depends on a free hyperparameter k (number of nearest neighbors); although sensitivity analysis shows relative stability, no principled guidance for choosing k in practice is provided.

Normalization of Clipped Density relies on a leave-one-out estimate computed from the real dataset itself (ClippedDensity_real), which could itself be affected by outliers or small sample sizes, creating a potential circularity/robustness concern not deeply analyzed.

The paper does not directly compare against compound single-value metrics like FID/FD-DINOv2 empirically, despite motivating the work partly by their lack of decomposability; such a comparison (e.g., correlation with human judgment relative to FID) would have strengthened the significance claim.

The manuscript is very long with a disproportionately large appendix (57 pages) relative to an 10-page main text, which, while thorough, may hinder self-containment and ease of review of the core contribution.
